utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: No. Not while I still went to school.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And later, just from seeing your statements, I noticed that your husband was also a waiter in the Panos company, and we know -- and did you know Mitar Vasiljevic through your husband?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And over how many years did you know who Mitar Vasiljevic was, just through your husband's experience?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: Many years.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And did you come to ever socialise with him to where you could have picked him out in a photo lineup or something like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: I saw Mitar Vasiljevic outside the police building during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And even seeing him outside the police, was there any trouble with you knowing who he was because of you being a resident of the community?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And other than him getting older with age, would you assume today that you might be able to recognise him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Were you ever asked to identify Mitar Vasiljevic as part of the investigation that you participated in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so when you came here in 2001 -- or not came here, but you were questioned in 2001, no one showed you pictures of any of the defendants?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: I was shown photographs, but I failed to identify anyone, but it was for reasons of personal safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I don't understand. What do you mean by that, "failed to identify ... for reasons of personal safety"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: I was waiting for this moment. I was waiting to see Milan and Sredoje here and to see them arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But do you think it would have assisted the Prosecution to know that you knew them by their photograph back in 2001?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, maybe I misunderstood. Can you tell me when you were shown photographs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, I mean, I only know because I only can see on paper that you were spoken to in 1998, and I can see that you were spoken to in 2001, and other than that I don't know of any other times. And so can you tell me if it was the first time you were spoken to by investigators or the second time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Can I ask you if the photographs of Milan Lukic and/or Sredoje Lukic were in those photographs and you simply did not look at -- want to identify them at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: I couldn't bear to look at the photographs. It was simply too hard.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, your birthday is in 1960. Is that about right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: No, that's not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I got it wrong, and I don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And if you need to move in private session, I have no objection. I want to preserve this witness' --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did you find it unusual that he, in the context of a first meeting, would give you the year of his birth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Because most -- I think that it's strange that someone would have to let you know what the year of their birth is when you first meet them. What did you think?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: I sure didn't ask him about his name, his last name, or his age.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so him saying "1967" was just out of the blue?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And this was part of the first time that you had ever met him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: Yes, the 26th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, if he was born in 1967, did he tell you anything about where he came from, or did you know this from the community?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, if he's only four years younger than you and it's a small community in Visegrad, had you ever heard of Milan Lukic in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But you had heard before the 26th of June that Behija Zukic had been killed by Milan Lukic, hadn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And before the 26th of June, had you heard anything else about a Milan Lukic from members of your Muslim community?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What kind of things did you hear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: That he was doing very bad things all over Visegrad and that he had been killing people, taking people away, raping people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, as part of these rumours about Milan Lukic, had you heard a description of him so you would know who to look out for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: No one described him to me. I just knew when he introduced himself that he was the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of the village of Rujiste?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did you ever come to know that Milan Lukic was from Rujiste, or his parents were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: People were saying that, but I didn't know that myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: How far is Rujiste from your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: I don't know. I've never been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that you knew who Sredoje Lukic was because he was a police officer; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And maybe a police officer as a public person might be someone you would have seen around the community for years before the war; wouldn't that be true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so even here today, taking in account for age and changes, you might -- if Sredoje Lukic were by himself, you might just be able to know him as someone you knew before the war; wouldn't that be true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so here today, even by process of elimination, you know that Milan Lukic is one of the persons charged in this room today, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: I recognise him, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you first about the Koric situation. You indicated that there was 10 to 15 refugees and you were with those refugees; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you indicated that the person -- that at first ten men, ten soldiers, entered the house asking for Hajra; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: That's what I heard from others. I didn't know myself. There was the Savic group that came first. I didn't know any of those. They said, "We could have killed all of you."

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And by "the Safic group," what does "Safic group" mean to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: Savic. Savic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Savic. And tell me about the Savic group.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: It was some sort of an army as well. Who were they after, what were they after, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Can you tell me if this Savic group was dressed in uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what kind of uniforms, if you could describe them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: Camouflage. Camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And there were different colours of camouflage at the time. Do you recall what kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Please describe them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: White and grey, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And -- now, you indicate that these ten men from the Savic group, they left, and Milan Lukic group came later; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And this is sometime between the 5th of July and the 1st of July; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And that's because you know the day you left Visegrad as being July 9th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And it -- it was within the next two or three days after you escaped from Bikavac, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And the only thing I'm asking you is, can you clarify, if you can, whether it was at the beginning of the 1st through the 5th or towards the end or in the middle, because -- in somehow relating it to when you escaped from either Bikavac or from Visegrad together. I'm sorry. I didn't hear your answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: It was between the 1st and the 5th. Whether it was on the 3rd, I can't say right now. I know it was at that time, and I am absolutely certain about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, when you say "Milan Lukic and his group," can you tell me how many men were in this group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: I didn't count them. I was too scared.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And when you were asked out of this house, you were exposed; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you're saying that Hajra Koric was in line with you and she was at the end of the line; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you say that Milan Lukic inspected this line, looking for Hajra; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And in your testimony today or in your statements before --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: My apologies. May I say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say Milan Lukic was looking. I said one of the men from his group was looking for Hajra. He walked up to my sister-in-law, and Milan said, "This isn't Hajra. There is Hajra." And then he took her aside.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so the next thing I was going to say and ask of you is that I do not see in your statements, nor did I hear from your -- from you today that Milan Lukic recognised you in this line or acknowledged you in any way.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: No one asked. I would have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: It doesn't appear that he was distracted by you or that he knew you from your statements or your testimony today.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you're trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, simply that I would expect, given the other things that you've testified about, that Milan Lukic might have made an issue about you and knowing you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: I recognised him, all right. His face is etched in my memory, and it will stay there forever.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I'm sorry, ma'am. You misunderstood me. I was more expecting that he would have recognised you and called you out or something to that effect at the time that Hajra Koric is being detained.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: He was looking for Hajra. The only thing he told me was, "Don't be afraid." When he finished with Hajra, I expected to meet the same fate as she. It was then that Milan ordered us to all go back to the house -- to our homes, rather, and that none of us were to leave our homes. And then he said that about 11.00 that evening he would be back to see us, and if anyone fled he would have everybody else killed. There was me and there was another lady. I can't say her name because we're in public session. We decided to leave the house, anyway, reckoning he couldn't kill everybody. Someone would make it and would live to tell the tale. We left the house -- we were in a house -- that evening, that night, at about 11.00, as far as I remember, we heard a huge clamor, some screaming and sounds of shooting. Was it Milan who was back to look for us? I really can't say. Perhaps you should ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, even so, it appears that he did not act as if he recognised you; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: How do you mean that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Just on that day, you say he only said, "Don't be afraid," but it doesn't appear that he singled you out in terms of recognising you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: He didn't single me out because I wasn't the one he was looking for. He was looking for Hajra Koric because what he wanted to do was to kill Hajra. Why? I really have no idea. Maybe you should ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, it's come to our attention you wouldn't -- and you would not have any reason to know this, but I want to put it in context, is that we have some information that someone else saw another person first shoot Hajra Koric and then -- described that a Milan Lukic shot second after she had already died. How -- can you explain that, or is there anyone that could believe that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did someone shoot Hajra Koric first and not Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: Milan Lukic shot Hajra Koric. No one else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did -- well, then that's, I guess, what I was going to ask you. Did somebody else shoot the body, too, that you saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: Do you understand what I'm telling you? I am telling you that Milan Lukic shot Hajra, and he was the only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I understand that, ma'am, but I'm going through some other statements that I've had to go through as part of this case, and you seem to be someone that could help clarify this for me, and that's why I ask you this question, not to offend you. Now, let's -- we can move on to a different subject. You indicate that VG-114 came to your doorway early in the morning of the 28th of June; is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And when you heard this banging on the door, can you describe it for the Court, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: VG-114 was banging at our door in order to wake us. It wasn't banging that was loud enough for the entire neighbourhood to be able to hear. It wasn't like she was trying to raise an alarm or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And am I clear from your testimony that you did not look at her, that you did not see her?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: I didn't dare to turn on the light. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so as you -- but how would you know it was her? How did you identify it as her?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: I know VG-114. I know her well. I also knew her parents very well, and nobody will tell me that it wasn't her. It was her voice. Before the war we socialised a lot, had coffee together a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what I did not see, though, in your testimony today nor your statements is description of any difficulties that she might have been having telling you this on that night.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: She told us coherently that Milan Lukic had set her on fire, together with his group, that she had tried to save her sister, who was aged 9 or 10, and she wasn't in good health; she was a little handicapped. She said, "My mother had burned to death, my two sisters, and the two children of my sisters. Save yourselves. Run for your lives." I understood very well what she told us that evening. She told us that her hands and arms had burned, that her hair had burned. I couldn't see her well because I didn't dare to turn on the light, as I said before. And that's what she said before she went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I guess the reason I ask this of you is because it's my understanding that her injuries were terrible, and it seems that she would have had difficulty moving around in such an injured state, and that's why I asked if you witnessed this.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: Esteemed counsel, she had such presence of mind, it's a miracle. That much I concede to you. In such panic, in such fear, she found the strength to go out and warn other people to save themselves. And if she had died of the injuries, somebody else would have lived to tell about what had happened, as I have made it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so you credit her with you leaving the village and making the decision to get out that night.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But -- now, when you first indicated that you saw a house burning outside the bathroom window, would it be fair to say that many Muslim homes were burnt at that time since the Uzice Corps came all the way through when you left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: I can't tell. That evening, that was the only house burning. Before that incident, other houses had burnt, but that evening it was Meho Aljic's house on fire. I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And -- but you only learned that later. You couldn't tell from the bathroom window that it was that exact house.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: Through my window, yes, I saw a house burning, and VG-114 told me personally that everybody in the house of Meho Aljic had been burned to death.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, when you mentioned that this was a Passat that had been there earlier, at least the Prosecutor mentioned that it was a Passat, and you understood it to be Behija Zukic's car; is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: Yes. Behija Zukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And the car that was -- earlier, that was Mr. Dzafic's, a Peglica, what colour was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: It was the colour of banana, if I remember well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yellow?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: Not quite -- typically yellow. It was not the standard yellow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm going to take the break at the usual time. It is now. There appears to be some uncertainty about the length of the breaks. The length of the evening session breaks are exactly the same as those for the morning: 20 minutes for the first break, and half an hour for the second. We should be concluding, though, in the evening at ten minutes after 7.00 in order to achieve equivalence with the morning session. So we will finish at ten minutes after 7.00 in the evenings when we do sit in the evenings. Let us adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Minor technical difficulty, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Madam, when we took a break, we were talking about the car of Ekrem Dzafic, and what was the colour of that car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: I said it was not the light yellow. Banana yellow, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And is that more of a bright yellow, like a hilighter pen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: Well, are you going to look for shades?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: If you can't remember, no, of course not. Now, let me ask you this question, ma'am. Is it true that many Muslims had their cars seized at some point or another during this aggression?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: So I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And if you know, is it true that many of these cars were taken to the police station for the use of these aggressors?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And is it true that you're saying that from the first time that you saw this Milan Lukic to later, that he was in fact in two cars?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: He drove me away in Ekrem's car.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And that is where you discovered a bottle of liquor; is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And was this bottle of liquor, was it half-drank? Was it almost empty? Was it almost full?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: I can't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I guess my next question would be, was the gentleman that you knew as Milan Lukic who took you in that car, was he intoxicated, or could you tell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: I couldn't tell. I was too afraid. I wasn't thinking of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, I guess at another point in time - and I'm kind of dancing around the subject - but you were with that person for two to three hours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not a good admission to make, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Pardon me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not a good admission to make, that you're dancing around the subject.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And isn't it true, ma'am, that "Lukic" as a last name is a pretty common last name in your part of the country?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And at a time with so many horrible things happening, there may have been more than one Milan Lukic in the Serbian army or amongst the Serbian aggressors; isn't that possible?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: There was only one Milan Lukic in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Isn't it true that there was another Milan Lukic, about 50 years old, that was a little more powerful in the community?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: Not that I know. I don't know that. I know only of this one that I pointed out today, and I'm certain 100 percent that it's him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But, ma'am, according to your 1998 statement, it appears that you were sure 100 percent that the person that you identified as Milan Lukic had blue eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think there's some misunderstanding about the statement in 1998. There was no B/C/S statement that the witness was able to read as was suggested a few questions ago. It's always done in English, and there was a translator translating back and forth between the witness and an investigator, who incidentally only speaks English as her second language. So I believe the proper question is what she remembers about his physical characteristics, not that she read a B/C/S statement and signed something that she was able to fully understand in her own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, didn't she give a statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, she gave it through an interpreter that was recorded by a person who, again, did not speak English as their first language. The question was put to her earlier on: Did she not have an opportunity to read her statement in B/C/S and in English in 1998? There was no B/C/S statement that she was able to read in 1998. She was dependent upon the interpreter. And as we've heard that our own very experienced interpreters here had great difficulty in one of the words she used in her description of Milan Lukic, it's quite possible that there was -- this is a translation problem and not a misdescription by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So what use can be made of a statement? Are you saying that not much use can be made of it in cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Not that not much use can be made of it, Your Honour, but the procedure that has been used certainly does have limitations, and it's wrong to suggest to the witness that she had an opportunity to read her statement in B/C/S and sign it. That never factually happened. She did not have a B/C/S copy in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, and the problem, I guess --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But she would have had an opportunity to hear it being read to her.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, through a translator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Through a translator, yes. Yes, Mr. Alarid. Perhaps you want to take that into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I would, but, one, with all due respect to Mr. Groome, he's sort of making himself a witness in terms of kind of, you know, giving us what was and what was the state of affairs when this witness statement was taken. But other than that, Your Honour, I think that maybe the point's been made, but I will ask the witness one more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Ma'am, isn't it true that you were read the statement in 1998 and given an opportunity to hear that before you signed the English statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: I did not get it in my hands because when I was questioned there was an interpreter who wrote it down, in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And, ma'am, but isn't it true that you initialed each page after it was read to you in succession?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: Yes, I put my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And by putting your signature on each page, that was you indicating that you understood what was being read to you and you agreed with it; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: The interpreter could have interpreted it, but I can't remember saying anything about blue eyes at all. I really can't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But isn't it true that the word for "blue" is very different than the word for "brown"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And we can see that because in the first paragraph of the Bosnian translation, it's clearly stated "blue eyes and light brown hair."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: "Dark brown hair," I said clearly, and I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I stand corrected. Dark brown hair. And do you consider dark brown being closer to black than blonde?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: It can't be close to blonde if it's dark brown.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And that's what I mean, ma'am. I want to know what you believe. If I were to tell you that someone had light brown hair, is that closer to blonde than black?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: Brown is brown. Dark brown. So it's closer to black than it is to light brown or to fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Could the court assistant please put on the screen --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And at this time, Your Honour, I would tender 1D10-1633 into evidence, the statement, 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's 1D44, Your Honours, under seal. It's 1D44, Your Honours, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And could the court usher please bring onto the e-court screen 1D00-3119.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I apologise. If we have exhibit number, it is not in the transcript, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is admitted as Exhibit 1D44 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Could the assistant even come a little closer into the face. Little closer, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And, ma'am, would it be fair to say that this picture is of the same gentleman that's in the courtroom today seated in the back room whom you identified earlier as the Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: That's him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And would you agree that the person's eyes in this photograph are brown, not blue?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And not wanting to quibble over light and dark brown, but I would argue that this is light brown hair. Would it be true that this is light brown hair?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree. It's dark brown. Plus, he may have dyed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: At this time, Your Honour, I would tender 1D00-3120 in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As 1D45, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And ma'am, I'm going to put another picture on the screen for you, and I trust me, I do not in any way mean to offend you, but it is this gentleman without a shirt on, and I'm going to put that on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Could we put 1D00-3111, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, ma'am, this may not be the best of pictures, and maybe the court usher could focus on the upper body, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When was this taken?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: It was taken after the war, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, ma'am, just looking at the picture, I don't necessarily see - and again, this could be my interpretation of things - but what would be characterised as birthmarks all over his body. I see some freckles, maybe, but I don't see birthmarks. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: Whatever you call them, freckles, birthmarks. He had spots on his body.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And would you characterise his hair in this photograph as light brown or dark brown?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: This picture, the hair is dark brown.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I would tender this into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As 1D46, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will continue for the -- I will continue for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Dieckmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Good evening, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: My name is Jens Dieckmann. I am Defence counsel for Mr. Sredoje Lukic. I just have a couple of questions to you, and I will put it in a manner to you with all respect to the pain you have suffered, I can assure you. I will try to put my questions as short and as precise as possible, and I would highly appreciate it if it would be possible for you to give, also, precise and short answers if it seems proper to you. Could we do it in this way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. First of all, do you agree with me that a human being is generally more capable to recall details of events that took place in recent times than events that occurred a long time ago? Could you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you mean. Can you please elaborate?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: I just want to ask you if, from a general point of view, isn't it more easily for a human being to recall details of events that took place in recent time, after a short time, than other events that occurred a long time ago?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: I see it all before my eyes now. In this courtroom, I'm seeing the whole thing again right before my very own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. VG-35, I put it to you that Sredoje Lukic was not present on the 27th June, 1992, in Bikavac, neither in the early morning, nor in the afternoon, nor in any other time on the day, because he was somewhere else far away from these events. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: I don't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that we have opposite answer, but my learned friend can check.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: I explain to you that -- I put to you -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, ma'am. Could you repeat your answer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: Sredoje Lukic was present. You can keep telling me he wasn't present. You can do whatever you like, but I know that he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. You know Sredoje Lukic being a policeman from Visegrad, true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And it happened in the time before the war that when you get off work, that you had seen Sredoje Lukic on a junction leading to Ciganija [phoen], walking to his home and wearing his police uniform. Is it true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: When you came from your work home, could you remember that you met Sredoje Lukic sometime when he passed your way wearing his police uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: I don't remember that because he was facing down to the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Do you remember that he was friendly greeting you when you passed him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-35
utterances.text: He used to greet me before the war. He knew my husband quite well, as I pointed out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And you know --

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And perhaps we could go in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 17th day of September, 2008, at 8.50 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.03 p.m.,
